content.title: Database indexes
content.prompt: Explain how database indexes work. Cover what they are, why they exist, and one tradeoff.
guiding_questions: What data structure is a typical index?
When does the planner ignore an index?

learning.short: An index is a separate data structure, usually a B-tree, that maps column values to row locations so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds reads at the cost of extra writes and storage.
learning.detailed:
Without an index, finding rows that match a condition means a sequential scan of every row. A B-tree index keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree with wide nodes, so lookup, range scans and ordering by the indexed column take logarithmic time. PostgreSQL also offers hash indexes (equality only), GIN (arrays, JSONB, full text), GiST and BRIN (very large naturally ordered tables).

Every insert, update or delete must also update each index on the table, so heavily indexed tables write more slowly and use more disk. The query planner uses statistics to decide whether an index is worth it: for a condition matching a large fraction of rows, a sequential scan is cheaper than random index lookups. Composite indexes matter in column order; an index on (a, b) serves queries on a or on a and b, but not on b alone. Covering indexes (INCLUDE) let the database answer a query from the index without touching the table.

In practice: index foreign keys and columns in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY of hot queries; use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm the index is used; watch for unused indexes and bloat.
key_points: B-tree gives O(log n) lookups and supports ranges and ordering.
Indexes cost write time and storage.
Column order in composite indexes matters.
Planner may skip an index when selectivity is low.
Partial and covering indexes reduce size and I/O.
Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, never guess.
examples: A phone book is an index on last name; finding by phone number still means reading every page.
Adding an index on orders(customer_id) turned a 4-second dashboard query into 20 ms.
common_mistakes: Indexing every column 'just in case'.
Assuming an index on (a, b) helps queries filtering only on b.
Forgetting that functions on a column (lower(email)) prevent index use unless the index is on the expression.
interview_questions: When would you use a partial index?
How does an index affect an UPDATE that does not touch the indexed column?
What is index bloat and how do you fix it?

content.title: Redis
content.prompt: Explain Redis: what it is, what it is good for, and where it is misused.
guiding_questions: What data structures does it offer beyond strings?
What happens to data on restart?

learning.short: Redis is an in-memory data store with rich data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams) used as a cache, message broker, rate limiter and lightweight primary store for hot data.
learning.detailed:
Redis keeps the whole dataset in memory and executes commands on a single thread, which makes it extremely fast and gives atomic operations without locks. Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots at intervals, AOF logs of every write, or both; neither turns Redis into a durable database with the guarantees of PostgreSQL.

Typical uses: caching query results with TTLs, sessions, leaderboards with sorted sets, distributed locks (with care), pub/sub, queues with lists or streams, rate limiting with INCR and EXPIRE. Lua scripting gives multi-step atomic operations. Redis Cluster shards keys across nodes; Sentinel handles failover.

Misuses: treating it as the source of truth for data you cannot lose, storing large blobs, unbounded keys without TTL (memory exhaustion), and using KEYS in production. Eviction policies (allkeys-lru etc.) decide what happens when memory is full.
key_points: In-memory, single-threaded command execution, atomic operations.
Data structures beyond key-value: sorted sets, streams, hashes.
Persistence is optional and not a substitute for a database.
TTLs and eviction policy are essential for caches.
Cluster for scale, Sentinel or managed service for HA.
examples: Session store for a web app with 30-minute TTL.
Sorted set leaderboard: ZADD on score, ZREVRANGE for top 10.
common_mistakes: Using Redis as the only store for orders or payments.
No TTL on cache keys, leading to OOM and eviction surprises.
Running KEYS * on a large instance and blocking it.
interview_questions: How would you implement a distributed lock and what can go wrong?
Compare Redis pub/sub with streams.
What is the difference between RDB and AOF?

content.title: Kubernetes
content.prompt: Explain Kubernetes to your chosen audience. What problem does it solve and what does it cost you?
guiding_questions: What is the control loop idea?
Pods, deployments, services: what are they for?

learning.short: Kubernetes is a container orchestrator: you declare the desired state (which containers, how many, how exposed) and its controllers continuously reconcile the cluster toward that state, handling scheduling, restarts, scaling and networking.
learning.detailed:
The core abstraction is the Pod, one or more containers sharing a network namespace. Deployments manage replica sets of pods with rolling updates; Services give pods a stable virtual IP and load balancing; Ingress routes external HTTP traffic; ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration; PersistentVolumes attach storage. Everything is an object stored in etcd, and controllers watch objects and act to close the gap between declared and observed state.

Benefits: self-healing, declarative deployments, horizontal scaling, portability across clouds, a huge ecosystem (Helm, operators, service meshes). Costs: significant operational complexity, networking and storage subtleties, YAML sprawl, and the need for people who understand it. Managed offerings (EKS, GKE, AKS) remove the control plane burden but not the application-level learning curve.

For small teams, a PaaS or a simple container service is often the better choice until scale or multi-service complexity justifies Kubernetes.
key_points: Declarative desired state plus reconciliation loops.
Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress are the everyday objects.
Self-healing and rolling updates come for free.
Operational cost is real; managed services help partially.
Not the right first choice for most small teams.
examples: A web app with three replicas: Kubernetes restarts a crashed pod and replaces a failed node automatically.
Rolling out v2 with a Deployment: new pods start, pass readiness probes, old pods terminate.
common_mistakes: No resource requests and limits, leading to noisy neighbours and evictions.
Missing readiness and liveness probes.
Adopting Kubernetes because it is fashionable rather than for a concrete problem.
interview_questions: What happens when a node dies?
How do you do a zero-downtime deploy?
How do you keep secrets safe in Kubernetes?

content.title: Docker and container images
content.prompt: Explain what Docker does and how image layers work.
guiding_questions: Why do layers matter for build speed?
What is the difference between an image and a container?

learning.short: Docker packages an application with its dependencies into an image and runs it as an isolated process (a container) using Linux namespaces and cgroups. Images are built in read-only layers that are cached and shared.
learning.detailed:
A container is not a virtual machine; it shares the host kernel and isolates the process view with namespaces (pid, network, mount) and limits resources with cgroups. This is why containers start in milliseconds and are lightweight.

Each instruction in a Dockerfile produces a layer. Layers are content-addressed and cached: if the instruction and its inputs have not changed, the cached layer is reused. Ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing (install dependencies before copying source) makes rebuilds fast. Multi-stage builds compile in one stage and copy only artifacts into a small runtime image. A container adds a thin writable layer on top of the image; changes there vanish when the container is removed, so persistent data belongs in volumes.

Good practice: pinned base images, non-root user, .dockerignore, small images (alpine or distroless when compatible), health checks, and scanning images for vulnerabilities.
key_points: Namespaces and cgroups, not virtualization.
Images are immutable stacks of layers; containers add a writable layer.
Layer cache depends on instruction order.
Multi-stage builds shrink images.
Data persists in volumes, not containers.
examples: Copying package.json and running npm install before copying the rest of the code keeps dependency layers cached.
The same image runs identically on a laptop and in CI.
common_mistakes: Running as root inside the container.
Baking secrets into image layers.
Giant images because build tools are shipped to production.
interview_questions: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT?
How would you reduce a 2 GB image?
Why might 'it works on my machine' still happen with Docker?

content.title: CAP theorem
content.prompt: Explain the CAP theorem and what it means for a real system you would design.

learning.short: In a distributed system experiencing a network partition, you must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error response). Partition tolerance is not optional.
learning.detailed:
Eric Brewer's conjecture, later proven by Gilbert and Lynch, applies to a specific model: linearizable consistency and always-available responses under arbitrary message loss. Because networks fail, real systems are either CP (refuse requests when they cannot guarantee consistency, e.g. ZooKeeper, etcd, a single-leader database that stops accepting writes without quorum) or AP (keep serving, possibly stale or conflicting data, e.g. Cassandra with low consistency levels, DNS).

The 'pick two of three' slogan is misleading: CA is not achievable in a distributed system, and the tradeoff only bites during partitions. PACELC extends the idea: during a Partition choose Availability or Consistency; Else choose Latency or Consistency. Most business systems are hybrid: strong consistency for money and inventory, eventual consistency for feeds, counts and caches.

Design implication: decide per data type what staleness is acceptable, and make the choice explicit in APIs (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) rather than discovering it in production.
key_points: Applies during partitions; partitions are inevitable.
CP systems sacrifice availability; AP systems sacrifice consistency.
PACELC adds the latency tradeoff in normal operation.
Consistency is a spectrum: linearizable, sequential, causal, eventual.
Choose per data type, not per system.
examples: Bank ledger: CP. Refuse the transfer rather than double-spend.
Shopping cart or likes counter: AP. Merge later.
common_mistakes: Claiming a system is CA.
Treating eventual consistency as an excuse for undefined behaviour.
Ignoring that a single-node database also becomes unavailable.
interview_questions: Is PostgreSQL CP or AP?
How does a quorum (W + R > N) relate to consistency?
What does 'read your own writes' require?

content.title: React reconciliation
content.prompt: Explain how React decides what to re-render and update in the DOM.
guiding_questions: What is the role of keys?

learning.short: React re-renders a component when its state or props change, produces a new element tree, diffs it against the previous one using heuristics (same type at same position, keys for lists), and commits only the minimal DOM changes.
learning.detailed:
A render is React calling your component function to produce elements; it is cheap but not free. The reconciler compares the new tree to the fiber tree from the last render. Elements of different types cause the subtree to be unmounted and rebuilt; same type means props are diffed and children are recursed. For lists, keys tell React which items moved, were added or removed; index keys cause state to attach to the wrong item after reordering.

Rendering is split into a render phase (pure, interruptible under concurrent rendering) and a commit phase (DOM mutation, effects). Parent re-render re-renders children by default; React.memo, useMemo and useCallback prevent unnecessary work when props are referentially equal. The React Compiler automates much of this memoization. Most performance problems are state placed too high in the tree, expensive work in render, or large lists without virtualization.
key_points: State change schedules a render of that component and its subtree.
Diffing is O(n) with heuristics: type and key.
Keys must be stable and unique among siblings.
Render phase is pure; side effects go in commit (effects).
Memoization prevents re-render only with stable references.
examples: Typing in a search box at the top of a page re-renders the whole page unless the input state is isolated.
Using array index as key in a sortable list swaps input values between rows.
common_mistakes: Mutating state in place so React sees no change.
Creating new object props on every render and wondering why memo does nothing.
Putting side effects directly in render.
interview_questions: Why are keys not needed for static children?
What changes with concurrent rendering?
When does useMemo hurt?

content.title: Flutter's widget, element and render trees
content.prompt: Explain Flutter's three trees and why rebuilding widgets is cheap.

learning.short: Widgets are immutable descriptions; elements are the long-lived instances that hold state and diff widgets; render objects do layout and painting. Rebuilding a widget usually just updates the existing element and render object.
learning.detailed:
When build runs, it returns a new widget tree. Each element compares its old widget with the new one using Widget.canUpdate (same runtimeType and key). If they match, the element keeps its state and calls update on its render object with the new configuration; if not, the element and its subtree are discarded and rebuilt. This is why GlobalKey and ValueKey matter when reordering children, and why changing a widget's type at a position resets state.

RenderObjects live in a separate tree and handle layout (constraints go down, sizes go up), painting and hit testing. Layout is single-pass and linear because parents pass constraints and children return sizes. Repaint boundaries limit how much repaints; relayout boundaries limit layout propagation.

Understanding this explains why const widgets skip rebuilds, why setState high in the tree is expensive, and why StatefulWidget state survives hot reload and rebuilds.
key_points: Widget: immutable config. Element: state and position. RenderObject: layout and paint.
canUpdate uses runtimeType and key.
Constraints go down, sizes go up, parent sets position.
Keys preserve state across reorders.
RepaintBoundary and const reduce work.
examples: Swapping a Container for a SizedBox at the same position drops the subtree state.
A list of stateful tiles reordered without keys shows the wrong state on the wrong tile.
common_mistakes: Thinking build is expensive per se; layout and paint usually dominate.
Using GlobalKey everywhere.
Holding state in widgets instead of State or an external store.
interview_questions: What is the difference between StatelessElement and StatefulElement?
What triggers markNeedsLayout vs markNeedsPaint?
Why is BuildContext actually an Element?

content.title: JWT vs sessions
content.prompt: Explain the difference between server-side sessions and JSON Web Tokens for authentication.
guiding_questions: Where is state stored in each?
How do you log someone out?

learning.short: A session stores login state on the server and gives the client an opaque id in a cookie. A JWT encodes claims in a signed token the client holds, so the server can verify it without a lookup. Sessions are easy to revoke; JWTs are stateless but hard to revoke.
learning.detailed:
With sessions, the server keeps a record (in memory, Redis or a database) and the browser sends the session id cookie. Revocation is deleting the record. Cookies should be httpOnly, Secure and SameSite to resist XSS and CSRF.

A JWT has a header, payload and signature. Anyone can read the payload (it is only base64), so it must not carry secrets; the signature (HMAC or RSA/ECDSA) proves it was issued by the server. Verification is local and fast, which suits distributed services and mobile clients. The price: a stolen token is valid until it expires, so use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, rotate refresh tokens, and keep a denylist for critical revocations. Pin the algorithm to avoid 'alg: none' attacks and rotate keys.

Many systems combine them: an auth service issues short-lived JWTs derived from a revocable session.
key_points: Session: server state, opaque id, easy revocation.
JWT: client-held signed claims, no lookup, hard revocation.
Never put secrets in a JWT payload.
Short expiry plus refresh tokens is mandatory with JWTs.
Cookie flags matter more than token format for web security.
examples: Traditional web app: session cookie in Redis.
Mobile app talking to microservices: JWT access token verified by each service.
common_mistakes: Storing JWTs in localStorage where XSS can read them.
Long-lived tokens with no revocation path.
Trusting the alg header from the token.
interview_questions: How would you implement logout with JWTs?
What is a refresh token rotation and why?
When would you use opaque tokens with introspection?

content.title: TLS handshake
content.prompt: Explain what happens when a browser opens an HTTPS connection.
guiding_questions: Symmetric vs asymmetric: which does what?

learning.short: The client and server agree on cipher suites, the server proves its identity with a certificate signed by a trusted CA, they establish a shared secret with a key exchange (ECDHE), and then encrypt the connection with fast symmetric keys.
learning.detailed:
After TCP (or QUIC) is established, the client sends ClientHello with supported versions, cipher suites and a key share. The server replies with ServerHello, its chosen parameters, its certificate chain, and its key share. The client validates the chain up to a root in its trust store, checks the hostname and expiry, and both sides derive the session keys from the Diffie-Hellman exchange. Only then does application data flow, encrypted with AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305.

TLS 1.3 removed weak options, made forward secrecy mandatory (ephemeral keys, so a leaked private key does not decrypt past traffic), and cut the handshake to one round trip, with 0-RTT resumption possible. Certificates prove identity, not trustworthiness; Let's Encrypt made them free and automated. Common operational failures are expired certificates, incomplete chains and mismatched hostnames.
key_points: Asymmetric crypto authenticates and exchanges keys; symmetric crypto carries data.
Certificate chain validated against the trust store.
ECDHE provides forward secrecy.
TLS 1.3: one round trip, fewer options, safer defaults.
Most outages are certificate management, not cryptography.
examples: Browser warning 'NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID' is an expired certificate.
A load balancer terminating TLS then talking plain HTTP inside the VPC.
common_mistakes: Confusing encryption with authentication.
Thinking HTTPS hides the hostname (SNI is visible unless ECH).
Pinning certificates in mobile apps without a rotation plan.
interview_questions: What is forward secrecy?
How does the client know the server owns the certificate?
What does mTLS add?

content.title: Idempotency in APIs
content.prompt: Explain idempotency and how you would implement idempotent payment requests.
guiding_questions: Which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition?
Where do you store it and for how long?

learning.short: An operation is idempotent if performing it several times has the same effect as performing it once. For APIs that create things, clients send an idempotency key so retries after timeouts do not create duplicates.
learning.detailed:
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST is not. Networks fail after the server has processed a request but before the client sees the response, so clients must retry, and retrying a POST /payments without protection charges the customer twice.

The standard solution: the client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it in a header. The server stores the key with the request fingerprint and the response; a repeat with the same key returns the stored response instead of re-executing. Keys should expire after a reasonable window (24 hours is common) and a reused key with a different payload should be rejected. Storage must be atomic with the operation (same transaction, or a lock on the key) to avoid a race where two identical requests both execute.

Idempotency also matters for message consumers and webhooks: process by event id and ignore duplicates.
key_points: Retries are inevitable; design for them.
Idempotency key: client-generated, unique per operation.
Store key, fingerprint and response atomically.
Reject key reuse with different payload.
Same principle applies to queue consumers and webhooks.
examples: Stripe's Idempotency-Key header.
A webhook handler that upserts by event id instead of inserting.
common_mistakes: Storing the key after executing the operation (race window).
Using the key globally instead of per user or tenant.
Treating PUT as safe to retry when it triggers side effects.
interview_questions: How do you handle a request in flight when a duplicate arrives?
What if the first request failed halfway?
How long do you keep keys?

content.title: Event sourcing
content.prompt: Explain event sourcing and when you would and would not use it.
guiding_questions: What is stored instead of current state?
How do you read current state efficiently?

learning.short: Event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event; current state is derived by replaying events. It gives a complete audit log and temporal queries, at the cost of complexity in reads, schema evolution and tooling.
learning.detailed:
Instead of updating a row, you append events like OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, OrderShipped to a per-aggregate stream. Rebuilding state means folding the events; snapshots avoid replaying long streams. Reads are usually served by projections (materialized views) updated from the event stream, which naturally pairs event sourcing with CQRS: separate models for writes and reads.

Benefits: full history for audit and debugging, ability to build new views from old events, natural integration with event-driven systems. Costs: eventual consistency between writes and read models, event versioning when business rules change, larger storage, and a steep learning curve. Deleting data (GDPR) is awkward with immutable logs and needs crypto-shredding or tombstones.

Use it where history is the product (ledgers, accounting, workflow engines). Avoid it for simple CRUD, or for teams without experience; a well-designed audit table often gives 80 percent of the value.
key_points: Append-only events are the source of truth.
State is a fold over events; snapshots optimize.
Projections serve reads (CQRS).
Great for audit and temporal queries.
Costs: consistency, versioning, deletion, complexity.
examples: A bank ledger where balance is the sum of transactions.
Git: commits are events; the working tree is a projection.
common_mistakes: Using events as the integration contract between services without versioning.
Querying by replaying streams instead of building projections.
Applying it to everything after one good experience.
interview_questions: How do you change an event's schema?
How do you handle a bug that produced wrong events?
How does this interact with the outbox pattern?

content.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
content.prompt: Explain RAG: the pipeline, why it exists, and its failure modes.
guiding_questions: What problem does it solve compared with fine-tuning?

learning.short: RAG retrieves relevant documents for a query and puts them in the model's context so the answer is grounded in your data. It avoids retraining, keeps information current and allows citations, but is only as good as retrieval.
learning.detailed:
Pipeline: ingest documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk into a vector, store vectors with metadata. At query time embed the question, find the nearest chunks (often combined with keyword search and a reranker), assemble a prompt with the top chunks and instructions, and generate an answer with citations.

Why not fine-tuning: fine-tuning changes style and skills but is poor at storing facts reliably, expensive to update and cannot cite. RAG updates by re-indexing. Failure modes: the right chunk is not retrieved (chunking too coarse or too fine, embedding mismatch, missing metadata filters), too many chunks dilute the context, the model ignores context and answers from memory, or the model hallucinates when context is insufficient. Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) separately from generation (faithfulness, answer quality).

Production concerns: access control on documents, freshness, cost of embeddings and tokens, latency, and observability of which chunks produced which answers.
key_points: Retrieve, then generate with context.
Chunking and embedding model choice dominate quality.
Hybrid search and reranking improve recall.
Evaluate retrieval and generation separately.
Access control and freshness are product requirements.
examples: Internal support bot that answers from the company handbook with links.
Code assistant that retrieves relevant files before answering.
common_mistakes: Chunking by fixed characters without regard to structure.
Skipping evaluation and tuning by anecdote.
Leaking documents the user is not allowed to see.
interview_questions: How would you decide chunk size?
When would you add a reranker?
How do you prevent answers from documents the user cannot access?

resources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
resources.author: Lewis et al.

content.title: Transformers at a high level
content.prompt: Explain how a transformer language model works, without equations.

learning.short: A transformer predicts the next token by turning tokens into vectors, letting every position attend to every other position to build context-aware representations, and repeating that in stacked layers. Training on vast text teaches it patterns of language and knowledge.
learning.detailed:
Text is split into tokens (sub-word pieces) and each becomes a vector (embedding) with positional information. In each layer, self-attention computes, for every token, a weighted mix of all other tokens' representations, where the weights come from how relevant each token is to the current one (queries, keys, values). Multiple attention heads capture different relationships. A feed-forward network then transforms each position. Residual connections and normalization make deep stacks trainable.

The model outputs a probability distribution over the next token; training minimizes prediction error over enormous corpora. Generation samples one token at a time, feeding it back in. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback shape raw next-token prediction into helpful assistant behaviour. Context windows limit how many tokens attention can see, and attention cost grows quadratically with length, which drives research into efficient attention and caching (KV cache) for inference.

Scaling laws showed that loss falls predictably with more parameters, data and compute, which is why frontier models are so large.
key_points: Tokens to vectors; attention mixes context; layers stack.
Next-token prediction is the training objective.
Instruction tuning and RLHF shape behaviour.
Context window and quadratic attention cost limit length.
Scaling laws drove model size.
examples: In 'the bank of the river', attention lets 'bank' use 'river' to resolve meaning.
KV cache is why the first token is slow and later tokens are fast.
common_mistakes: Saying the model 'looks up' facts in a database.
Confusing tokens with words.
Assuming larger context always means better answers.
interview_questions: Why is inference memory-bound?
What is the difference between pretraining and fine-tuning?
Why do models hallucinate?

content.title: Blue-green and canary deployments
content.prompt: Explain blue-green and canary deployments and how you would choose between them.
guiding_questions: What is the rollback story for each?
What do you measure during a canary?

learning.short: Blue-green runs two identical environments and switches traffic all at once, giving instant rollback. Canary shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches metrics, and ramps up, catching problems with limited blast radius.
learning.detailed:
Blue-green: deploy the new version to the idle environment, run smoke tests, flip the router or load balancer. Rollback is flipping back. Costs: double infrastructure during the switch, and any database schema change must be compatible with both versions at once (expand and contract migrations).

Canary: route 1–5 percent of traffic to the new version, compare error rate, latency and business metrics against the baseline, then increase in steps or roll back automatically. Requires good observability and traffic splitting (service mesh, load balancer weights, feature flags). It catches issues that only appear with real traffic. Feature flags decouple deploy from release entirely and allow per-user rollouts.

Choose blue-green for infrequent, well-tested releases where instant rollback matters and traffic splitting is hard; choose canary (with automated analysis) for frequent releases in systems with enough traffic to make small percentages meaningful. Both require backward-compatible data changes.
key_points: Blue-green: whole switch, instant rollback, double capacity.
Canary: gradual traffic shift, metric-driven, smaller blast radius.
Database changes must be compatible across versions.
Feature flags separate deploy from release.
Observability is a prerequisite, not an add-on.
examples: Flipping a DNS or ALB target group between two ASGs.
Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts analysing error rate at 5, 25, 50, 100 percent.
common_mistakes: Running a destructive migration during blue-green.
Canary percentages too small to produce statistically meaningful signals.
No automated rollback criteria.
interview_questions: How do you handle sessions during a blue-green switch?
What metrics would abort a canary?
How do you canary a mobile app?

content.title: Connection pooling
content.prompt: Explain database connection pooling and why serverless apps struggle without it.
guiding_questions: What does a pooler like PgBouncer do?

learning.short: Opening a database connection is slow and each one consumes server memory, so applications keep a pool of open connections and reuse them. Serverless functions scale to many instances that each want connections, overwhelming the database unless a shared pooler sits in between.
learning.detailed:
PostgreSQL forks a process per connection, costing several megabytes and setup time. A pool inside the application keeps N connections open and hands them to requests. Sizing: a small pool (roughly cores × 2 plus disk spindles as a starting heuristic) usually outperforms a large one because the database serializes work anyway.

With serverless or many app replicas, the total connections multiply. PgBouncer or a managed pooler multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few server connections. Session pooling keeps a server connection per client session; transaction pooling reuses connections between transactions, which is more efficient but breaks features that assume a persistent session (prepared statements by name, SET commands, advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY).

Symptoms of missing pooling: 'too many connections' errors, high latency from connection setup, and database CPU spent on connection churn.
key_points: Connections are expensive; reuse them.
Small pools are usually faster than large ones.
External poolers multiplex many clients onto few server connections.
Transaction pooling breaks session-level features.
Serverless multiplies the problem.
examples: A Next.js API on serverless hitting max_connections at traffic spikes until a pooler is added.
Pool size 10 outperforming pool size 100 under load in benchmarks.
common_mistakes: Creating a new client per request.
Setting the pool size equal to expected concurrent requests.
Using named prepared statements behind transaction pooling.
interview_questions: How do you size a pool?
What happens when the pool is exhausted?
How do you pool across many serverless instances?
